items.title: 68089_John Malachi oral history interview
items.q: I named Leo Parker and Illinois, of course, and Joe Newman, and Illinois' brother, Russell, and of course, the three men in the rhythm section

ctx.x: beginning, the upper-left-hand-corner to the lower-right-hand-corner, he was purely concentrating on what he was doing. And which any musician like that, particularly a drummer, gives a band a spark, then it becomes contagious. It makes guys play, you know!

Oh, I forgot to mention the other person in the band that was very significant. I don't know how I missed him. It was J.J. Johnson. I kept thinking back, counting the people that I named. I named Leo Parker and Illinois, of course, and Joe Newman, and Illinois' brother, Russell, and of course, the three men in the rhythm section, and all the while I was thinking there had to be somebody else.

And that other person was another real spark in the band, J.J. Johnson, who was really... He was young and into his... To me, he was at his peak of playing. And he was playing like non one else then. There are trombone players since then who seem to have caught on to his method, and a lot of them have became very proficient in it. But at that particular time, no one was playing trombone like J.J. Johnson. In talking to him and talking to other trombone players, he had gotten a whole new concept of playing. I…
